text.p: A shock fall in U.S. payrolls sent the dollar zig-zagging out of the morning's tiny ranges, only to wind up little changed from where it began the European day.

September non-farm payrolls came in down 40,000, confounding market expectations of a 166,000 rise and a far cry from August's 241,000 increase. But analysts noted that hourly earnings ticked up, as did the average work week.

U.S. bonds jumped in response to the data, but the dollar was less convinced. "The foreign exchange market doesn't honestly know what to do with it," said Graham Cocks, vice-president, treasury at Bank of Boston here.
The U.S. currency was quoted at 1.5290/95 marks by 1402 GMT compared to late Thursday's European level of 1.5293/98 and Friday's opening of 1.5305/10.
It dipped initially after the data emerged before jumping on the Treasuries bandwagon to ride to a session high of 1.5333. But as U.S. bonds retraced slightly, so did dollar/mark.
Dollar/yen was more placid, sticking stubbornly within a session range of less than 30 ticks to stand at 111.50/55 yen in late trade compared to Thursday's close here of 111.45/50.
"I've never seen any good link between payrolls and the currency markets, ever," said UBS economist Peter von Maydell.
"Basically this confirms and validates everything the Fed's been doing," said Von Maydell, who is senior currency economist at UBS in London.

Analysts said the payrolls data sharply reduced the chances that the U.S. Federal Reserve would hike interest rates at its next policy-making meeting on November 13. The decision to hold rates steady at last month's meeting took many by surprise.

The September increase in average hourly earnings raised concerns, however, and market watchers said forthcoming U.S. CPI, PPI and employment cost data would be closely watched for signs of any unsettling tick-up in prices.
"A potential fly in the ointment is on the prices side," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank.

U.S. Labor Secretary Robert Reich told Reuters Financial Television he saw no sign of wage-push inflation despite the hourly earnings rise. Asked about the jobless rate, which rose to 5.2 percent from August's 5.1, he said it could still fall.

Market watchers remained broadly bullish on the dollar, and were encouraged by its success in sticking above 1.5260 marks support. But some were concerned by its inability to rally better on the back of strengthening bonds and by a noteworthy swoop down by dollar/Swiss after the U.S. employment report.
The dollar hit a session low of 1.2515 Swiss francs after the data but had recovered to 1.2555/65 by 1457 GMT compared to an opening level of 1.2538/43 and Thursday's close of 1.2560/70.
"If we're going to get a continued dollar move higher I'd expect the Swiss to continue weakening first," said Cocks at Bank of Boston.
"The dollar doesn't appear to have the strength to power it forward -- I think all we're going to do is stagger from one trading range to another," he added.
European high yielders, whose recent strength against the mark has been a major dollar-positive, remained firm.
The stars of the show were the Italian lira and Finnish markka, buoyed as speculation of their imminent entry into the European exchange rate mechanism tore through the market.
Italy's Prime Minister Romano Prodi said today he wanted "immediate, rapid" talks with European partners on the level at which lira might rejoin the ERM.
In Germany, August industrial orders rose 0.6 percent from July, the third consecutive monthly increase, but slowed slightly from July's 0.9 percent rise.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8968
